/society/2026/oct/26/carers-allowance-cl.headline: Chancellor scraps 'unfair' cliff-edge rule that punished unpaid carers
/society/2026/oct/26/carers-allowance-cl.bodyHtml:
The controversial rule that led to unpaid carers being punished with penalties amounting to thousands of pounds is to be abolished, the Guardian can reveal.

The chancellor, John Healey, is to announce a new digital taper system for carer’s allowance in Wednesday’s budget, effectively ending what is regarded as one of the UK benefit system’s most feared and unfair administrative practices.

The scandal was highlighted in a Guardian investigation that revealed how hundreds of thousands of carers have, through no fault of their own, run up life-changing debts in recent years after overstepping weekly earnings thresholds by just a few pence.

Those hefty debts were then ruthlessly chased down by welfare officials who pursued carers using legislation designed to recover funds from drug dealers and organised crime bosses. Some unpaid carers were convicted of fraud as a result.

The cliff-edge rule dictates that if a carer earns even a penny more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – they forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, currently £86.45. A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40.

Although the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) was aware when carers breached earnings limits, it refused to warn them, insisting the onus was on carers to report any changes.

Thousands of carers spent long periods unaware of the breach, in some cases for years, resulting in overpayment debts typically of £2-£5,000 but in some cases as much as £20,000.

Under new rules set to be announced in the budget, the introduction of a tapered system instead of a cliff-edge means only £1 of carer’s allowance will be removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit, meaning carers are no longer left financially worse off for working additional hours or receiving a pay rise.

The announcement is one of five more “everyday fixes” announced by Healey ahead of his budget on Wednesday. His room for manoeuvre is severely constrained by the tight fiscal backdrop, a result of global events including the conflict in Iran.

Treasury insiders have warned that the budget will be low-key, with difficult tax and spend decisions put off until the spending review next year. But there is anxiety among some Labour MPs over the scale of the announcements, after Andy Burnham came to power promising major change.

Among the other measures to come is making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent – with the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles locked in, and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles to 35p per mile. The Treasury said the move would benefit about 3 million people – employees and self-employed – who use their own vehicle for work.

The chancellor’s intervention on the draconian cliff-edge rule comes after an award-winning Guardian investigation which revealed how the DWP had for years known of the profound distress it caused carers – including warnings from a DWP whistleblower – but did nothing about it.

The Guardian’s reporting triggered a government-commissioned independent review of carer’s allowance overpayments by disability rights expert Liz Sayce, published last year. It found unpaid carers suffered depression and hardship on a huge scale after falling foul of a series of systemic injustices, including the cliff edge.

In one case highlighted by the review, a carer was penalised when the national minimum wage had increased at a faster rate than the earnings limit. This put her 15p a week above the limit, even though her hours had not changed. Months later, she was told she had incurred a £2,000 penalty for above-limit earnings totalling just £5.

The review found the outdated design of carer’s allowance, coupled with longstanding DWP failures in its administration, meant about 180,000 carers ran up overpayment debts amounting to £300m between 2019 and 2025.

Campaigners welcomed the decision, calling it a “long-overdue reform” although there was disappointment the technical demands of building a new digital system to run the taper means it will not be introduced before the end of the decade.

Carers UK said the cliff-edge plays havoc with carers’ attempts to work part-time around their minimum 35 hours a week of caring duties, with many giving up paid work or refusing promotions, overtime or bonuses because of the risks.

John Healey, the chancellor, told the Guardian the carer’s allowance system had worked against carers. “That means doing an extra shift or getting a small pay rise can actually leave someone worse off. That cannot be right.

“So at this budget on Wednesday, we’re ending that cliff-edge. Carer’s allowance will instead taper as earnings increase, giving carers the freedom to work a little more and earn a little more without suddenly losing all their support.”

As well as unpaid carers, Healey’s budget will benefit an extra 150,000 new parents – including self-employed fathers and partners who have previously missed out – with parental support worth up to £194 a week.

Ministers are also removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on paraffin.

There will also be hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, to make it more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue.

Healey will also reportedly raise the minimum wage by about 4% to about £13.20 an hour. However, in a sign of government concern over rates of youth unemployment, the chancellor is said to be about to raise youth rates by roughly the same amount, rather than the inflation-busting levels seen in previous budgets.

Labour came to office in 2024 promising to raise the youth rate, which applies to workers under 21, to the same level as the full rate. But ministers have become concerned in recent months that raising the minimum wage for younger workers could be dissuading companies from taking on young employees.

“We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn’t mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren’t fair,” Burnham said.

“If you’re a nurse driving to work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket.”

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said: “We have listened to [carers’] concerns about the cliff-edge built into the system which leaves them financially worse off for taking on a few more hours, or getting a modest pay rise, and intend to bring that to an end.”

Kirsty McHugh, chief executive of Carers Trust, said: “It is great news that the government is acting to remove the carer’s allowance cliff-edge. This is an important and long-overdue reform.

“We would urge the government to use this change as a springboard for a wider and deeper reform of carer’s allowance – a benefit that remains stuck in the 1970s and must be made fit for the future.”

Emily Holzhausen, Carers UK director of policy, said: “We have countless stories from carers who have shared their deep fears of going just a few pence over the earnings limit and losing all of their benefit.

“It’s absolutely right that the chancellor is thinking of practical changes that will make their lives easier. A taper on the earnings limit should give families much more choice about working and still caring.”

/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.headline: Lula wins historic fourth term in Brazil after dramatic comeback
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.bodyHtml:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return to Brazil after winning a historic fourth term in power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro.

“This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.

A few hours earlier, Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from a first-round defeat in early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff.

“Today is a historic day,” Lula declared, before telling a sea of elated supporters: “Democracy always, dictatorship never again. Democracy always, fascism never again.”

Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.

But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo and cities all across Brazil. He won with 64.2m votes to Bolsonaro’s 59.8m, a 51.79% to 48.21% victory. It was at least 10m more votes than Lula secured in the first round.

While Bolsonaro initially refused to concede, his party acknowledged the election results on Monday, nearly a full day after Lula’s win.

“We recognize the presidential election results,” Liberal party head Valdemar Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.“

Lula’s health minister, Alexandre Padilha, told the Guardian shortly after the result was confirmed: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defence of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed.

“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha said at the hotel where the president’s team was following the count in São Paulo.

Bolsonaro rejected the result, following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.

The US administration had been rooting for a Bolsonaro victory that would have seen the pro-Donald Trump so-called “orange wave” continue its sweep across the region into Latin America’s largest democracy. Trump took almost 24 hours to comment and, on Monday, appeared to endorse Bolsonaro’s claim when asked about Brazil’s election.

“It looked terrible to me. I thought it was a terrible look. I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election, frankly,” the US president said.

When asked if he intended to do anything in response, Trump said: “Well, I’m not running Brazil. I’m running the USA. And I just thought that the election was – I like Lula. I get along with him very well. I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated. The extension given was very strange.”

Other leaders and governments from across the political spectrum were quicker to recognise Lula’s victory. Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum, tweeted: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, wrote: “The global progressive resurgence has just begun.”

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called Lula’s victory “a historic win for the global progressive movement” and said his government looked forward to continuing to collaborate on “shared values of democracy, social justice and climate action”.

Rightwing South American leaders also recognised Lula’s victory, with Chile’s president, José Antonio Kast, calling Lula to offer congratulations and Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, saluting “the Brazilian people for this democratic day”.

Even Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella – who had publicly backed Bolsonaro and appeared in a recent live broadcast with him on social media – acknowledged Lula’s win, tweeting: “When the people decide at the ballot box, their will is respected because it is sacred. That’s what democracy is all about!”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.”

A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said: “China respects the choice of the Brazilian people.”

Besides Trump, one of the few powerful international voices of dissent was Elon Musk, who claimed the “math doesn’t add up” for Lula’s comeback, ignoring the fact that it did because of the historically low level of abstention in the second round.

In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the US had been accused of seeking to influence the result through a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure. Erika Hilton, a transgender lawmaker who recently became the most voted-for woman in Brazil’s congress, said those efforts had failed. “We have defeated the interference of the US government, which thought it could turn our country into its back yard. Brazil and the Brazilians are too gigantic to be anybody’s back yard,” she said.

Lula’s victory will also have profound consequences for the environment and the Amazon rainforest in what is the world’s most biodiverse nation. On the eve of the vote, the former environment minister Marina Silva had warned that Bolsonaro, if elected, would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rainforest destruction started by his father, whose 2019-22 administration coincided with a surge in deforestation.

On Sunday night, Silva was in a buoyant mood, telling the Guardian: “My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people.”

She said: “The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations.”

For Flávio Bolsonaro, the future looks bleak. As the scale of Lula’s victory became clear on Sunday night, the mood at the Brasília mansion where Bolsonaro was watching the count soured, with what had initially resembled a lively birthday party turning into something closer to a wake. Like football supporters heading for the exits midway through the second half because their team was being thrashed, crestfallen guests began heading home.

One of them approached the dozens of journalists waiting for Bolsonaro’s speech to shout that it was the “north-east’s fault”, insulting the region where Lula has historically won most of his votes.

One photograph circulated by Lula supporters showed a dejected Bolsonaro in tears, although it had been taken on the eve of the vote. Another image showed a red-faced Bolsonaro flanked by visibly mortified allies as they came to terms with their defeat. São Paulo’s pro-Bolsonaro governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, sat next to him covering his face with his hand.

On Paulista Avenue, where huge crowds had gathered to hear Lula speak, one reveller wore a costume of Flávio Bolsonaro behind bars. Some suspect the senator is likely to flee the country to the US once his term runs out in February and he loses parliamentary immunity. Bolsonaro is facing a series of federal police investigations over suspected misdeeds including money laundering, although he maintains he is innocent.

Lula supporters delighted in the idea that the far-right politician may soon join his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his coup attempt, in jail.

“Oh, how awful! Poor little thing!” João Maluf, a 27-year-old psychologist, shouted sarcastically as he held up his mobile phone to the crowd to show them a photograph of a visibly distraught Bolsonaro. “We want rid of these fucking Bolsonaros,” Maluf said.

/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.headline: Bank of Israel rebukes Netanyahu over sanctions-evasion claim
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.bodyHtml:
Netanyahu has forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual US military aid would dry up soon, and has drawn a rare public rebuke from Israel's central bank over a separate, repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions. “Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”

The rebuke came as Netanyahu resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran, as his far-right coalition narrowly trailed in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.

Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran. Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.

Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports, but insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.

Netanyahu posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation. “Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.

On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February. The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.

Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring. In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.

Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.

The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.

As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”

He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.

The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.

The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.

The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.

In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”

The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.

In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.

Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.

His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.

Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.headline: Report urges Wednesday's budget to restore child benefit's value for stretched families
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.bodyHtml:
Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow, is urging the chancellor, John Healey, to use Wednesday's budget to make good on Andy Burnham's pledge that his would be a "cost of living government". "Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children," she said.

Patrick leads Changing Realities, an online project tracking 100 low-income families, and her long-term study shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.

Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn't pay, according to Patrick. She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants in the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.

One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: "It's getting to a point where I don't know how we are going to keep managing to run our car." She added: "Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled."

The report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants, of which 67 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month. Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem.

The report comes as the British Retail Consortium said shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, warning that "the dam is starting to break" when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.

The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.

It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on Healey before his first budget on Wednesday. Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.

The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month.

Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.

Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank's nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year.

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: "The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years." She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.

The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.

/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.headline: Burnham vows not to move ahead of the British public on EU ties
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.bodyHtml:
Downing Street moved to calm confusion over Andy Burnham's position on freedom of movement with the EU, after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue. A spokesperson said Burnham was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option.

“He is saying that it’s time for us to discuss what kind of long-term relationship with Europe is best for Britain and he is referring to the types of areas that that agreement and long-term future could cover,” the spokesperson said. “He is crucially not leaning either way, and that will be for the British public to decide. And his focus for now is on next month’s summit and the practical arrangements that we hope to make there, which will add billions to the economy.”

Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels.

Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue.

The spokesperson said the government was not yet at the stage of confirming whether the public would decide on proposals for the UK to move closer to the EU.

Asked whether Burnham accepted that returning to freedom of movement would mean Britain lost control over legal migration, the spokesperson said: “He’s not setting out a concrete position either way. What he’s saying is that he wants to have a conversation with the British public about what our long-term future with the European Union looks like.”

In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about how the UK can move closer to the EU.

On Monday, Burnham ruled out the possibility of rejoining the EU within this parliament and indicated he could fight the next general election on a promise to take the UK back into the EU. He said: “I’m not going to move away from the red lines that were in the Labour manifesto.”

Hours later, Burnham told journalists “no” when asked if he would allow the UK to join the EU freedom of movement scheme without a referendum.

When asked whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he said: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”

Challenged on how his constituents in Makerfield would feel about his discussions about the EU, given 65% of them voted to leave, Burnham added: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing. The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation to Brexit.”

Burnham even ruled out an early general election on a manifesto change on this issue. He told GMB: “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” However, he left the door open to a future fight on a promise to fully rejoin the EU.

Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit on 20 November, as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. He believes the Brexit deal has “weakened our economy [and] weakened our control of immigration” and is not good enough for the country.

/uk-news/2026/oct/26/russell-brand-trial.headline: Former assistant tells Russell Brand's rape trial his behaviour went unchallenged
/uk-news/2026/oct/26/russell-brand-trial.bodyHtml:
Russell Brand, 51, who faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999, sat still in the dock at Southwark crown court on Monday as statements from prosecution witnesses were read to the court. Wearing a grey suit and white shirt, he denies all the charges.

Helen Berger, who worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when he was at the height of his fame, told the court the job was one of the hardest she had had because Brand had "non-stop energy", and she left because she was "sick of him" and burnt out.

In a May 2024 witness statement to police, Berger alleged Brand had an "insane sexual appetite" and that his bad behaviour was "normalised and dismissed" by those around him.

Berger alleged she had seen Brand treat women badly and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend walking in on him having sex with someone in his dressing room.

She also told the court she had overheard the comedian receiving oral sex in a toilet cubicle and once found a celebrity leaving his bedroom in the morning.

"Though I'd worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level. I think everyone else normalising and dismissing Russell's behaviour made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is," Berger said in the statement.

Describing his behaviour, she added: "He was always in his underwear, he loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on. I remember Sadie Frost came over to interview him. He did the whole interview in his underwear and no shirt and an open robe."

At the time, Brand had filming commitments for Channel 4's Big Brother as well as MTV and the BBC, a radio show, a national comedy tour, a weekly Guardian column, and was writing a book.

"In addition to his busy work, he had an insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night. He was very open about what his needs were," Berger said in the statement, which was read out by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC.

"He never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed," Berger alleged. "There were times when I was at his house and he would be on a deadline … and he would get antsy and joke with me: 'May I go and have sex now?'"

She recalled Brand turning to the website Myspace to find random women to sleep with and how women, including an unnamed celebrity, would often be at his flat in Camden, north London, for sexual liaisons. "He was like a peacock, women always approached him," she said.

When Brand was recording an MTV show, Berger alleged, he told her to ask women for their phone numbers, which she said made her feel uncomfortable.

She alleged that on other occasions she had to keep Brand's mother and girlfriend away from his dressing room because he was having sex, and she overheard him receiving oral sex in a women's toilet. Berger described overhearing Brand talking and recognising his trademark cowboy boots in the cubicle next door.

Berger recalled that when Brand was headlining the Edinburgh festival, he ended his show by asking that anyone with "a vagina and heartbeat" meet him at a pub afterwards. Many women showed up, Berger said, and she later found him having sex in the shower at the apartment he was renting.

"I never witnessed Russell doing anything against the law," she said, before adding: "I did see Russell treat women poorly."

She recalled how he was once "hitting on" a woman who revealed she had a boyfriend, before Brand "turned in a way" that startled his then PA. "He literally just switched off his charm and moved on to the next woman," Berger said.

The court also heard a witness statement from the manager of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Brand when she worked at Channel 4 in 2009. The manager said she recalled the alleged victim telling her that Brand's associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy had "told her she had to give Mr Brand a massage" or he would not continue with the day's recording.

The manager recalled being told that Bayles and Roy "were both there the whole time and watched and laughed while Mr Brand sexually assaulted her right in front of them".

The sister of a woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted and then orally raped by Brand at a Soho bar in 2004 told the court she was "upset and almost in shock" the next morning.

In 2023, the woman called her sister in tears and told the "full story" of what had happened, the court heard.

"It sounded like she was struggling to catch her breath," the witness recalled. "She said his [Brand's] eyes had gone completely black and he was possessed or had been a completely different person."

The trial continues.

/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.headline: Home Office commits to publishing evaluations of its asylum AI tools
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.bodyHtml:
The Home Office says it has already committed to publishing updated evaluations of the AI tools it uses, and that trained caseworkers, not AI, make decisions on asylum claims, after a report found the technology has been embedded across the department in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Use of artificial intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims.

“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their rollout.”

Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”

Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to the report by Open Rights Group (ORG).

It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.

Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour's Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party's Pete Wishart and the Green party's Siân Berry.

The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.

It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.

The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.

Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications. It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.

Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”

/uk-news/2026/oct/27/meghan-duchess-of-s.headline: Junior MasterChef Australia taps Meghan to co-host alongside Poh Ling Yeow in 2027
/uk-news/2026/oct/27/meghan-duchess-of-s.bodyHtml:
The Duchess of Sussex is set to co-host Junior MasterChef Australia, the children’s version of the popular televised cooking competition, in 2027.

Meghan made her debut appearance on the adult version of MasterChef Australia in July this year, which was filmed during a four-day visit to Australia with Prince Harry in April. Network 10 said the Duchess’s appearance on the show drew its “largest Sunday audience since 2023”.

Now the broadcaster has confirmed Meghan will co-host Junior MasterChef Australia, the children’s version of the show with contestants aged between nine and 13.

No date has been set for production, which will take place at Melbourne Showgrounds.

“I had an incredible time with the whole team at MasterChef this past April, so when they approached me to come back and work with this young group of talent, it was an easy yes,” the Duchess of Sussex said in a statement.

“I love cooking with my own kids, so seeing what these young stars create in the kitchen is going to be a lot of fun. I can’t wait to see what they cook up!”

It is unknown whether it means a temporary relocation to Australia for Meghan, Prince Harry and their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. The family relocated to the UK in August, after living in California for six years.

Meghan will host Junior MasterChef Australia with current MasterChef Australia judge Poh Ling Yeow, who will continue to judge the adult show in 2027 as well.

“I had a lovely time filming with Meghan earlier this year, and being reunited will be a real treat,” Yeow said in a statement. “I can’t wait to meet our pint-sized culinary adventurers.”

The news of Meghan’s next television appearance comes in the same week the Duchess of Sussex revealed she had been made aware that her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, had been accused of possessing child sexual abuse images.

Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities in the Philippines last week alleging that he had discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images at his father’s former home there.

Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick” and “a bunch of lies”. He claimed the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025.

The allegations against Markle Sr are currently being investigated by a human trafficking and child sexual exploitation taskforce in Cebu, authorities have confirmed.

On Sunday, Meghan revealed in a statement through her spokesperson that the Met had made her aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2019.

“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” she said.

The Sussexes are reported to have settled in the Cotswolds after leaving the US. In September, they condemned the “reckless intrusion” of two photographers who were spotted outside Archie and Lilibet’s school. Their children have since moved schools.

The Duchess of Sussex’s lifestyle show With Love, Meghan ran for two seasons on Netflix. It has been widely reported that the show won’t return for a third season despite Netflix reporting it was viewed 5.3m times globally in the first half of 2025.

/football/2026/oct/26/harry-kane-ends-en.headline: Harry Kane wins the Ballon d’Or, football’s most prestigious prize
/football/2026/oct/26/harry-kane-ends-en.bodyHtml:
Harry Kane is the Ballon d’Or winner for 2026, the first Englishman to win football’s most prestigious individual trophy in 25 years.

Two hours into a lavishly excitable ceremony at the Palladium Theatre in London, Kane’s name emerged from the final envelope to wild cheers inside the auditorium. The women’s Ballon d’Or, awarded moments earlier, was won by Alexia Putellas of London City Lionesses, a third Ballon, five years on from her first in the colours of Barcelona.

In the men’s voting, Kane finished ahead of co-favourites Lamine Yamal of Barcelona and Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid, an outcome that will perhaps cause the familiar consternation among the hierarchy of those clubs, not to mention the vast online fan army attached to the superstar players in Kane’s wake.

But Kane is also a fully deserving winner of football’s ultimate gong. The L’Équipe-sponsored trophy is awarded by a vote of journalists and administrators across the footballing super-scape. For Kane, it is reward for a year during which he has won the European Golden Boot, played a major role in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga title, captained England to a World Cup semi-final, and above all shown himself to be a wonderfully humble superstar player.

“It was really tough this year, the incredible players I was up against,” Kane said as he received the trophy, going on to congratulate everyone else nominated for anything else, and thank pretty much everyone he has ever played with.

“I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special,” he added.

As a pure goalscorer, his numbers are astonishing this year, with 89 goals for club and country since the start of August 2025. At Bayern, Kane has also become a darling of the Bundesliga for his all-round game, creativity, intelligence and professionalism. Bayern paid a record €100m fee up front for Kane three years ago, a transfer that broke the club’s usual recruitment patterns and raised some concerns, given Kane was 30 at the time.

It is a measure of his contribution on and off the pitch that this outlay is now seen as entirely vindicated. As a Ballon d’Or winner, Kane now enters rarefied company, heir to a prize that revolved around the Messi-Ronaldo two-hander for so many years, and which promises not just a form of sporting ultimacy but a vast uplift in current and future commercial earnings.

More widely, the award is a coronational moment for Kane himself, 16 years into a professional career that has taken in loan spells at Leyton Orient and Millwall, running himself into the ground to make it in the Premier League, and now, for posterity, into the lineage of elite footballers.

Earlier this month, Kane equalled England’s all-time caps record, while nudging his international goal tally on to 91 in 125 appearances. Aged 33, he still has a home Euros two years from now in his sights as England’s captain and a final opportunity for a different kind of footballing immortality.
